title: Why exchange rates go up and down
examples: Why does a currency get stronger?

left.label: Buyers of rupees
left.ask: Why does a currency get stronger?

explain.say: Going on holiday from India to Thailand, you swap rupees for baht. But why do you get more baht in some years than others? An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. Look at the board: buyers of rupees on one side, sellers on the other.

draw.text: Why exchange rates go up and down

left.label: Buyers of rupees
left.ask: Why does a currency get stronger?

explain.say: Look: when foreign tourists visit India, or foreign firms buy Indian software, they need rupees. More buyers make that side heavier, so the rupee rises, which means each rupee buys more foreign money. Can you think of another reason people want rupees?

left.label: Tourists, exports
left.ask: Why does a currency get stronger?

explain.say: Now the other side. When India buys oil from abroad, it sells rupees to get dollars. More rupees for sale makes the rupee fall. See the seesaw tip the other way? What else does India buy a lot of from abroad?

So is a strong currency good? Look at both sides. A strong rupee makes imports and trips abroad cheaper but Indian exports pricier for others. A weak rupee does the opposite. Which would an exporter prefer?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Neither is simply good or bad

explain.say: Interest rates, news and confidence move the seesaw too, every second of the day. Great thinking! Wow: about 7.5 trillion US dollars of currencies are traded every day, making it the biggest market in the world.

left.label: Buyers of rupees
left.ask: Why does a currency get stronger?

faq.a: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, such as how many rupees you need to buy one US dollar or one Thai baht.

faq.q: Why does a currency get stronger?
faq.a: When more people want to buy it, for example to pay for a country's exports, to visit as tourists, or to invest there because interest rates are higher.
It depends who you are. Shoppers and travellers like a strong currency because imports and trips are cheaper; exporters and tourism businesses prefer a weaker one.
For most big currencies, the market sets them through buying and selling. Some countries fix or manage their rate instead, and central banks sometimes buy or sell currency to steady it.
asks: Does the government set exchange rates?

faq.q: What is a fixed exchange rate?
faq.a: A fixed or pegged rate is held at a set level by the central bank. The Saudi riyal has been pegged at 3.75 to the US dollar since 1986.

facts: The Bank for International Settlements found about 7.5 trillion US dollars a day of foreign exchange trading in 2022.
The Saudi riyal has been pegged at 3.75 riyals to the US dollar since 1986.
